title: 0436-hockey-player-performance-via-regularized-logistic
universal_lens: The primitive unifies high-dimensional event attribution across sports via L1-regularized logistic regression. By modeling binary outcomes (e.g., scoring) as a function of sparse player-presence indicators and unpenalized situational covariates, it isolates marginal individual contributions from systemic confounders, establishing a universal partial-effect operator for discrete state transitions.
gsi_mapping: GSI maps this to a hierarchical Bayesian framework where the L1 penalty acts as a Laplace prior. This yields posterior distributions over player effects, enabling conformal prediction intervals for future performance. The unpenalized team/situation terms absorb structural biases, ensuring robust out-of-sample inference on true talent levels.
gse_mapping: For GSE, the model operates as a situational state-transition engine. Each play is a discrete event governed by current game-state covariates. The regularized logistic kernel computes the probability of favorable state changes (EPA/WPA), dynamically adjusting player valuations based on real-time contextual dependencies and opponent interactions.

primitives.name: Partial Scoring Effect Operator
primitives.verbatim_quote: Method / model Logistic regression on "which team scored goal i" (Equation 1): log[q_i/(1-q_i)] = α + u_i′γ + v_i′φ + x_i′β_0 + (x_i ∘ s_i)′(β_s + p_i β_p).
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: q_i: dimensionless probability of home scoring; \alpha: dimensionless intercept; u_i: team-season indicator vector; \gamma: team effect coefficients; v_i: special-teams indicator vector; \phi: situation coefficients; x_i: player presence vector (-1, 0, 1); \beta_0: baseline player effect; s_i: season interaction; \beta_s: season innovation; p_i: playoff indicator; \beta_p: playoff innovation.
primitives.assumptions: Conditional independence of goal events given covariates; linear additivity in the logit space; correct specification of situational controls.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Standard MLE fails due to high dimensionality (p >> n) and extreme sparsity of player configurations (median ~8 seconds), leading to perfect separation or non-invertible design matrices.

layer2.mapping: Isomorphic to NFL EPA-per-snap attribution. The logistic link models the probability of positive expected points added, while player-presence vectors map directly to roster alignment indicators on a specific down.
layer2.telemetry: Correlation between estimated partial effects and realized EPA/WPA metrics.

primitives.name: Lasso Confounding Control Kernel
primitives.verbatim_quote: Estimation: L1 (lasso) penalized negative log-likelihood (Equation 4), penalizing ONLY player effects (β_0, β_s, β_p); team-season (γ) and special-teams (φ) unpenalized to fully remove confounding.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: \theta: parameter vector; P(y_i|x_i, \theta): likelihood of outcome; \lambda: dimensionless regularization strength; \beta_j: player-specific coefficients subject to L1 penalty.
primitives.assumptions: True player effects are sparse or shrinkable toward zero; team and situational effects are dense and structurally necessary, requiring no shrinkage.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Breaks down if highly correlated player pairs (collinearity) exist without sufficient variation, causing arbitrary sign flipping among teammates unless group lasso variants are applied.

layer2.mapping: Derives a clean signal kernel by mathematically projecting out team-strength and situational variance. In GSE, this isolates the pure skill component from environmental noise.
layer2.telemetry: Reduction in residual variance compared to unpenalized OLS or raw plus-minus.

primitives.name: Partial Plus-Minus Metric Generator
primitives.verbatim_quote: Derived metrics: partial for-% PFP_sj = (1+exp[-β_0j-β_sj])^-1 (Eq 5); partial plus-minus PPM_sj = g_sj(1-2·PFP_sj) (Eq 6), same scale as PM but controlling confounders.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: PFP_sj: dimensionless partial for percentage; \beta_0j, \beta_sj: estimated player log-odds; g_sj: number of goals observed in configuration s with player j.
primitives.assumptions: The logistic transformation accurately reflects the underlying generative process of scoring probabilities; exposure (goals witnessed) scales linearly with the metric.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Singularities occur when exposure g_sj approaches zero, inflating the variance of PPM despite stable PFP estimates.

layer2.mapping: Directly maps to adjusted plus-minus metrics in other domains. It translates abstract log-odds into an intuitive, exposure-weighted impact score usable for market valuation.
layer2.telemetry: Alignment with external market proxies like player salary or contract value.

reasoning_traces.think:
The core mathematical derivation begins with the recognition that standard maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) collapses in high-dimensional, sparse settings typical of modern sports analytics. With thousands of players and fleeting on-ice configurations, the design matrix is overwhelmingly sparse, leading to perfect separation and infinite coefficient estimates. To resolve this, the authors introduce an L1-penalized logistic regression framework. The objective function minimizes the negative log-likelihood augmented by a Laplacian penalty strictly applied to player-specific coefficients. Crucially, covariates representing team-season strength and special-teams situations remain unpenalized. This dual treatment allows the model to fully absorb macro-level confounding variables—such as coaching quality or home-ice advantage—into the unpenalized intercepts, while aggressively shrinking noisy, low-exposure player effects toward zero. The resulting estimator yields a 'partial' effect: a player's isolated contribution to the log-odds of a scoring event, conditional on the precise lineup and game state. From these log-odds, the framework derives intuitive metrics like Partial For Percentage (PFP) and Partial Plus-Minus (PPM). PFP represents the probability of the player's team scoring given their presence, while PPM scales this probability by actual exposure, mirroring traditional plus-minus but purged of teammate/opponent bias. The duality here lies in balancing bias (via shrinkage) against variance (via confounder control). Failure modes emerge primarily from collinearity; if two elite players always appear together, the L1 penalty may arbitrarily assign the entire effect to one, zeroing out the other. Furthermore, the assumption of conditional independence ignores temporal autocorrelation in momentum, though this is often secondary to the massive gains from confounder removal.

reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: This methodology traces its lineage to the foundational work on Adjusted Plus-Minus (APM) by Duhon et al., which utilized ridge regression to solve multicollinearity in hockey. Gramacy, Taddy, and Tian advanced this by adopting L1 regularization (Lasso), recognizing the inherent sparsity of player impacts and the need for variable selection. Historically, it bridges classical econometric fixed-effects models with modern high-dimensional statistical learning, moving sports analytics from descriptive box-score aggregation to causal, context-aware attribution.
reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: From a theory of mind perspective, the model implicitly reconstructs the decision-making environment of coaches and general managers. Coaches construct lineups to maximize scoring probability against specific opponents; the unpenalized situational terms capture these strategic constraints. General managers allocate salaries based on perceived marginal value. By correlating the derived partial effects with actual salary data, the model reverse-engineers the market's implicit valuation function. It assumes agents act rationally to exploit talent differentials, and the model successfully extracts these differentials even when obscured by the chaotic, interactive nature of team sports.
reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: A critical cross-layer veto condition arises regarding data leakage and anti-collinearity. If team-strength effects are not perfectly captured by the unpenalized covariates, residual confounding will leak into the penalized player coefficients, artificially inflating the ratings of players on dominant teams. Additionally, extreme collinearity among star players can cause unstable rankings; the L1 norm tends to select one variable from a highly correlated group, potentially misattributing shared success. Therefore, any transfer of this primitive to new domains (like NFL snap-level data) must rigorously validate that situational controls (down, distance, score differential) are sufficiently rich to prevent team-strength leakage into individual player priors.
